The capacity-vs-SLA problem

A 200 A PDU rated for steady-state server load has different effective capacity under a GPU load with elevated harmonic content. Heating from 5th and 7th harmonic THD reduces real headroom. Your spec sheet doesn't capture that.

One zone has legacy CPU racks, the next has a GPU tenant pushing 120 kW racks. The transformers, switchgear, and paralleling between them see a load profile no one designed for. Harmonic stress accumulates on equipment rated for clean sinusoidal current.

Per-zone capacity numbers from your monitoring don't reflect the shared-infrastructure penalty above. When the tenant deploys and a protection event happens, you're explaining a downtime credit to a customer with competitive alternatives a phone call away.

Three tenant zones (legacy 8 kW CPU, mixed, GPU-dense 130 kW) feed a shared paralleling bus and upstream transformer. As the tenant mix shifts, the shared bus sees changing harmonic profile (H1, H5, H7) AND changing RMS current (1× to 15× of legacy baseline). The transformer is stressed differently at each extreme: K-class limit at 100% legacy, amperage limit at 100% GPU.

[Movie Review] 'On the Day the Verdigris Dawns' (1) | Thoughts on Japanese Entertainment Since the COVID-19 Pandemic
It feels as though it depicts the state of entertainment after the COVID-19 pandemic, and I felt it was a story that could only have been born in modern-day Japan.

The long-established Tatewaki Fireworks Factory is being forced to relocate due to town redevelopment. Keitaro Tatewaki, who grew up there, has been struggling alone to complete the legendary firework known as <Shuhari> in place of his father, who vanished. On the last day of summer, Kaoru, a childhood friend living in Tokyo, returns to their hometown.
In Japan today, entertainment has fully recovered. Attendance at music concerts and movies has bounced back, and it is even said that the numbers have grown beyond what they were before the pandemic.
Through the COVID-19 pandemic, Japanese entertainment has evolved and become resilient. (Of course, there are fields that were weeded out as a result, and I have complicated feelings about that.)
I felt that 'On the Day the Verdigris Dawns' depicts the path that such Japanese entertainment has followed.
Perhaps it was a story that could only be depicted by Director Yoshitoshi Shinomiya, who also has a face as a Japanese-style painter.

It is the feature-length directorial debut of Japanese painter Yoshitoshi Shinomiya and a joint Japanese-French production. The film was officially selected for the competition section of the Berlin International Film Festival.

Then, his childhood friend Kaoru (voiced by Kotone Furukawa), who lives in Tokyo, returns after four years. Dragging in Keitaro's older brother Sentaro (voiced by Miyu Irino), who works at the city hall, the three make a plan to create and launch fireworks in their final two days.

However, I do not want to dismiss this film as 'just another youth anime.' This is because the 'gaze' that Director Shinomiya has cultivated as a Japanese painter transcends the skeleton of the story and shakes the very senses of the viewer.

The phantom fireworks 'Shuhari.' This is not just the name of a firework. It is the very philosophy of 'Shu-Ha-Ri' (protect, break, detach) that director Yoshitoshi Shinomiya inherited from the tradition of Japanese painting.

In the climax launch scene, the blue that spreads across the night sky is not just any color. The actual Japanese painting pigment called Verdigris (Hanarokusei) is a 'poisonous blue' made from copper. It shines beautifully, but if handled incorrectly, it can corrode the skin.
The reason Kaoru returned from Tokyo also connects here. Because of a past incident (a childhood accident at the factory), she had chosen to 'detach.'

Director Shinomiya values the 'space between the lines' as a Japanese painter. I believe the scarcity of dialogue and the abundance of silence are devices to project the viewer's 'own scenery' onto the film.

In fact, Verdigris changes color and becomes more toxic when oxidized. The director, who has been researching Japanese painting materials for many years, says, 'Beautiful things are always precarious.'
Reviews tend to dismiss it as 'all about the visual beauty,' but I feel differently. This blue might be the very 'poison of lost tradition' that modern Japan carries.
What is repeatedly mentioned in director interview magazines is the 'lost landscape.' The project started in 2016. In 10 years, Shinomiya's own environment, family, and Japan have all changed.

This is a fantastic masterpiece titled 'From Ancient History' by the avant-garde artist Jiro Kimura, who was born in Hyogo.

Jiro Kimura was born in 1936. Since his high school years, he has repeatedly won selections and awards at various public exhibitions and art group shows. While he received high praise from art professionals and curators, he deliberately chose not to pursue the path of a professional painter, instead maintaining his own unique creative activities.
As a result, his works are extremely rare in the market, and he remains a figure known only to those in the know.
As the title suggests, this work is themed around 'ancient history,' but it does not depict specific ruins or figures.
